Karl Marx. A nineteenth century German philosopher and economist whose theories of historical materialism and class struggle provided the intellectual foundation for communism and socialism.

Marx published The Communist Manifesto in 1848 with his collaborator Friedrich Engels, a passionate call to revolution. But his major work was Das Kapital, published in 1867, a massive critique of capitalist political economy that took him decades to write. It remains one of the most influential books ever written, though arguably one of the least read.

Marx developed the theory of surplus value. Workers produce value. They add to raw materials through their labor. But capitalists pay workers only a fraction of the value they create. The difference between what workers produce and what they receive as wages is surplus value, which capitalists appropriate as profit. This is the secret to capitalist accumulation and also, Marx argued, the root of its exploitative nature.

He championed historical materialism, the idea that economic systems and the class relations within them drive the course of history. Great ideas and great individuals matter less than the underlying economic structures. These economic structures inevitably change as technology advances and contradictions accumulate.

Marx predicted that capitalism contained internal contradictions that would drive it toward collapse. Overproduction, falling profit rates as competition intensifies, concentration of wealth into fewer hands, worker impoverishment. Eventually, he believed, these contradictions would become unbearable and the working class would revolt, establishing a classless communist society.

He made a conceptual move that proved enormously influential. He distinguished between labor-power, what workers sell to capitalists, and labor, what workers actually perform. This distinction revealed the exploitative nature of wage work. You sell your capacity to work for eight hours, but the capitalist extracts ten hours of effort, pocketing the difference.

Marx built his analysis partly in dialogue with Adam Smith, refuting the invisible hand narrative. He adopted David Ricardo's labor theory of value and his theory of falling profit rates. Twentieth century critic John Kenneth Galbraith shared Marx's skepticism about unregulated markets, though Galbraith rejected Marx's revolutionary conclusions in favor of reform.
